title: Christ, the King and Head
blurb: Church government begins with a claim about Christ, not with a theory of organization.
text: christ, the king and head church government begins with a claim about christ, not with a theory of organization. the book of church order does not open with courts, officers or procedure. it opens with jesus christ, on whose shoulders the government rests, who holds in himself every office of the church, and who rules and teaches his church from his throne through his word and spirit by the ministry of men. that last phrase carries the weight of everything that follows. ministers are the means through whom a living king acts. they are not successors who hold his place while he is away. the lord jesus, as king and head of his church, hath therein appointed a government, in the hand of church officers, distinct from the civil magistrate. christ executeth the office of a king, in calling out of the world a people to himself, and giving them officers, laws, and censures, by which he visibly governs them. the preface says christ has given his church officers, oracles and ordinances, and has ordained in it a system of doctrine, government, discipline and worship, either set down in scripture or deduced from it by good and necessary inference, with nothing to be added and nothing taken away. two consequences follow at once. church power is service, not invention: all of it is only ministerial and declarative, because scripture alone is the rule of faith and practice. and no officer may claim authority or titles of spiritual pre-eminence beyond what scripture uses. the book calls the representative or presbyterian form of government scriptural, and says it is necessary to the perfection of the order of the visible church. it then adds that it is not essential to the church’s existence. that limit is not politeness. it is why the same book can recognise other denominations as true branches of the church of jesus christ wherever they maintain the word and sacraments in their fundamental integrity. a church that thinks its order is scriptural, and also thinks a church with weaker order is still a church, is not being inconsistent. it is holding both 1-1 and 1-7. order exists for the sake of the people. examinations guard who teaches. sessions give every member named shepherds. courts above the session mean no congregation is left alone with its worst moment, and no officer is the last word on his own case. read the rules that follow as answers to one question: how are the people christ has gathered to be taught and governed in faithfulness to him.

title: Who Runs the Church
blurb: Four standing answers to the question of who governs, and where the Presbyterian answer differs.
text: who runs the church four standing answers to the question of who governs, and where the presbyterian answer differs. every church answers a practical question: when a decision has to be made, who decides, and who may review it. the historic answers fall into a small number of families. episcopal. authority runs through bishops, understood as an order above presbyters. ordination and oversight belong to the bishop, and congregations are governed through him. single-elder congregational. the congregation holds final authority and is led by one pastor, with deacons serving. associations of churches are voluntary and advisory. plural-elder congregational. the congregation still holds final authority, but is led by a plurality of elders rather than a single pastor. presbyterian. the people elect elders; the elders govern jointly in courts; and the courts are connected, so that a lower court is subject to review by a higher one. a fourth question cuts across all of them: does the civil power govern the church. the westminster confession as received in the pca answers no. civil magistrates may not assume to themselves the administration of the word and sacraments; or the power of the keys of the kingdom of heaven; or, in the least, interfere in matters of faith. against episcopal government, the book teaches that bishop, pastor, presbyter, elder and teacher name one office and not different grades, and that ordination is ordinarily the act of a court rather than of a man. against congregational government, the book lodges jurisdiction in the session rather than in the congregation, and makes every court answerable upward. the congregation’s own power is real but defined: it elects officers, calls its pastor, and acts on its property. presbyterian government is not congregational government with elders added, and it is not a mild episcopacy. the difference in both directions is jurisdiction: who may judge, and who may review the judgment.

title: The Marks of Presbyterian Government
blurb: Six features that make a church presbyterian, each with the section of the book that carries it.
text: the marks of presbyterian government six features that make a church presbyterian, each with the section of the book that carries it. christ alone is head. the church has no other, and every officer acts under his law. plurality. jurisdiction is not a several but a joint power, exercised by presbyters in courts. one elder alone is not a court, and a church with only one ruling elder and no pastor has no session. parity. elders hold one office. ruling elders have the same authority and the same eligibility to office in the courts as teaching elders, and every court is a presbytery in the sense that it is made up only of presbyters. representation. the people elect those who rule. no man may be placed over a church in any office without the election, or at least the consent, of that church. connection. courts are graded, each with exclusive original jurisdiction over what belongs to it, and each subject to review and control above. the courts are not separate tribunals: every act of jurisdiction is the act of the whole church through the appropriate organ. spiritual power only. church courts are wholly distinct from the civil magistracy, have no jurisdiction in political or civil affairs, and can impose no temporal penalty. each mark limits a different danger. plurality limits the man who would rule alone. representation limits the court that would rule without the people. connection limits the congregation that would answer to no one. spiritual power limits the church that would reach for the sword. where elders differ: some hold that scripture prescribes this order by divine right in every detail, others that it is the best reading of scripture while leaving more room in the details. the book itself calls the form scriptural and stops short of calling it essential to the church’s existence.

title: How This Book Came To Be
blurb: A line from Geneva and Scotland through Westminster and colonial Philadelphia to Birmingham in 1973.
text: how this book came to be a line from geneva and scotland through westminster and colonial philadelphia to birmingham in 1973. geneva, 1541. calvin’s ecclesiastical ordinances set out four orders of ministry, pastors, doctors, elders and deacons, with a consistory of ministers and elders for discipline. scotland, 1560 and 1578. the first book of discipline and then the second book of discipline, associated with andrew melville, set the parity of ministers, rule by elders in graded assemblies, and the independence of the church’s government from the crown. westminster, the 1640s. the assembly produced a form of presbyterial church-government and a directory for public worship alongside the confession of 1646 and the catechisms of 1647. 1706. the first presbytery in the colonies was organised at philadelphia with francis makemie. the exact date cannot be fixed because the first leaf of its minutes is lost. 1716 or 1717. the first synod. archives differ: the presbyterian historical society dates its creation to 1716, and the pca historical center to 1717. 1729. the adopting act. the synod received the westminster confession and catechisms as its standards in all essential and necessary articles, and left the presbytery to judge differences over interpretation. the 1740s and 1758. the old side and new side divided over revival and ministerial standards, and reunited in 1758. 1788 and 1789. a constitution was adopted, the presbyterian church in the united states of america was formed, and the confession was revised at 20.4, 23.3 and 31.2, which removed the civil magistrate from ecclesiastical matters. the first general assembly met in 1789. 1861. on december 4 the southern church was organised, later named the presbyterian church in the united states. 1936: the orthodox presbyterian church was formed in june, called the presbyterian church of america until 1939. on december 4 to 7, 1973, at briarwood presbyterian church in birmingham, alabama, elders representing about 260 congregations with over 41,000 communicant members organised the national presbyterian church. the founding date was chosen to match the southern church’s own founding date in 1861. the name was changed to presbyterian church in america in 1974, at the second assembly at macon, georgia. in 1982 the reformed presbyterian church, evangelical synod joined the church. the church reported for 2025: 87 presbyteries, 1,673 churches and 286 mission churches, 5,388 teaching elders, 317,773 communicant members, and a total membership of 405,634 counting communicants, non-communicants and teaching elders. much of the wording in this book is older than the denomination that uses it. the optional forms printed at the back come from the southern church’s book of 1893 and the orthodox presbyterian book of 1940, which is a small sign of a long inheritance.

title: A People Taught and Judged
blurb: Before there are church courts there is a people who must be taught, and elders who must judge.
text: a people taught and judged before there are church courts there is a people who must be taught, and elders who must judge. israel is a people brought into life with god and then taught how to live before him. azariah describes the dark alternative in three absences: without the true god, without a teaching priest, and without law. order fails where teaching fails. the book keeps the same order. the visible church before the law, under the law and under the gospel is one and the same, which is why the elders of israel stand behind the ruling elder of a congregation. moses cannot carry the people alone. jethro’s counsel and the appointment of the seventy put judgment in the hands of able men who fear god, and the hardest cases still travel upward. two features of later polity are already visible: shared rule, and graded review. the charge given to those judges is a charge about impartiality: hear the small and the great alike, do not be intimidated, and remember that the judgment is god’s. church courts inherit that charge. elders act for the people at the passover, in covenant renewal, in war, and in disputes at the gate. the office is representative before it is administrative, which is why the book grounds the ruling elder in it rather than in a modern committee. the parallel is not an argument that israel had presbyteries. it is that god has long governed his people through appointed men who judge in his name and answer to him for it.

title: The Shepherd Who Rules
blurb: In the Gospels the King who governs is the Shepherd who saves, and he gives his church the authority to judge.
text: the shepherd who rules in the gospels the king who governs is the shepherd who saves, and he gives his church the authority to judge. jesus is not presented as the ablest administrator of an existing religious order. he forgives sins, reveals the father, gives life, and answers the question of what is lawful by his own authority as lord of the sabbath. church government stands downstream of that. he also exposes an order that had become unfaithful, where tradition displaced the commandment and position was sought for its own sake. officers are warned by this, not exempted from it. to peter and then to the disciples jesus gives the keys of the kingdom, and binds and looses through the assembled church. the confession puts this in the hands of church officers. to these officers the keys of the kingdom of heaven are committed; by virtue whereof, they have power, respectively, to retain, and remit sins; to shut that kingdom against the impenitent, both by the word, and censures; and to open it unto penitent sinners, by the ministry of the gospel; and by absolution from censures, as occasion shall require. the steps of matthew 18 are written into the rules of discipline: personal admonition, then one or two witnesses, then the church acting through her court. the steps must be followed in order, and a person wronged may not prosecute a personal offense without first trying the means of reconciliation christ requires. the same passage sets the tone: the flock is sought, the little ones are guarded, and forgiveness has no arithmetic limit. discipline is the work of a shepherd, not of a prosecutor with a caseload.

title: Churches Learning to Decide
blurb: Acts and the letters show elders appointed, an assembly deciding, and order given for the sake of life.
text: churches learning to decide acts and the letters show elders appointed, an assembly deciding, and order given for the sake of life. paul and barnabas appoint elders in every church; titus is left to appoint elders in every town. the elders of a single congregation are always plural, and the same men are called elders and overseers in the same breath. the book reads those titles as the scriptures use them: as descriptions of the duties of one office rather than as ranks. a dispute at antioch is not settled at antioch. it goes to the apostles and elders at jerusalem, the assembly deliberates, its decision is sent to the churches, and the churches are strengthened by it. the confession takes acts 15 as warrant for assemblies commonly called synods or councils. for the better government, and further edification of the church, there ought to be such assemblies as are commonly called synods or councils. the same chapter sets the limits that the book keeps: such assemblies determine controversies of faith ministerially, may err, and are to handle nothing but what is ecclesiastical. deacons appear where the care of widows threatened the ministry of the word, and the apostles refuse to abandon either duty. qualifications for overseers and deacons are written down. gifts are given with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. a congregation in disorder is told to let all things be done decently and in order. the risen lord then addresses churches directly, commending, rebuking and calling to repentance. officers who hear those letters learn that the lord judges the institution as well as those inside it.

title: The Preliminary Principles
blurb: Eight principles stand in front of the Form of Government and set the spirit in which its rules are read.
text: the preliminary principles eight principles stand in front of the form of government and set the spirit in which its rules are read. 1. god alone is lord of the conscience. it is left free from doctrines and commandments of men that are contrary to the word, or that in matters of faith and worship are not governed by the word. the right of private judgment in religion is universal and inalienable, and no religious constitution should be supported by the civil power beyond the protection given equally to all. 2. every church, or union of churches, may declare its own terms of admission, the qualifications of its ministers and members, and its whole internal government. it may err by making those terms too lax or too narrow, but in doing so it misuses its own liberty rather than infringing the liberty of others. 3. christ has appointed officers not only to preach and administer the sacraments but to exercise discipline, for the preservation of both truth and duty. officers, and the whole church in whose name they act, must censure or cast out the erroneous and scandalous, keeping the rules of the word in every case. 4. godliness is founded on truth, and a test of truth is its power to promote holiness. faith and practice, truth and duty, are inseparably joined. 5. those admitted as teachers must be sound in the faith, yet there are truths and forms about which men of good character and principles may differ. in these, private christians and churches owe one another mutual forbearance. 6. scripture lays down the character, qualifications, authority and manner of investiture of church officers, but the power to elect persons to the exercise of authority in a particular society rests in that society. 7. all church power, whether exercised by the body in general or by representation, is only ministerial and declarative, since scripture is the only rule of faith and practice. no church judicatory may make laws to bind the conscience. all courts may err, yet it rests on them to uphold the laws of scripture. 8. ecclesiastical discipline is purely moral or spiritual and carries no civil effect. its force comes only from its own justice, the approval of an impartial public, and the countenance and blessing of the great head of the church. the section closes by saying that where these principles are steadily held, the vigour and strictness of government and discipline, applied with pastoral prudence and christian love, will serve the glory and wellbeing of the church. principle 5 stands behind the stated differences a court may allow at licensure and ordination. principle 6 stands behind congregational elections. principle 7 limits what an assembly deliverance can claim. principle 8 explains why a church court can only admonish, suspend, depose and excommunicate, and can never fine or imprison. god alone is lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are, in anything, contrary to his word; or beside it, if matters of faith, or worship. these principles descend from the constitution adopted by american presbyterians in 1788. the line of descent is standard in the histories and was not checked against the 1788 text here.

title: What the Constitution Is
blurb: Two documents make the Constitution, and not everything printed with them is part of it.
text: what the constitution is two documents make the constitution, and not everything printed with them is part of it. the constitution is subject and subordinate to the scriptures of the old and new testaments, the inerrant word of god. it consists of the doctrinal standards, that is the westminster confession of faith with the larger and shorter catechisms, together with the book of church order, which comprises the form of government, the rules of discipline and the directory for worship. the appendices, which include suggested forms for marriages, funerals, discipline and terms of call, carry no constitutional authority and are printed for information. the rules of assembly operations govern how the assembly does its business and are likewise not part of the constitution. the directory for worship is a special case. a statement adopted by the third general assembly calls it an approved guide, to be taken seriously as the mind of the church, which does not have the force of law and is not obligatory in all its parts. chapters 56, 57 and 58 were later given full constitutional authority, and so was section 59-3. so a session that departs from chapter 51 on music is exercising liberty within a guide. a minister who departs from 59-3 on marriage is departing from the constitution. deliverances, resolutions, overtures and judicial decisions of the assembly are to be given due and serious consideration by the church and its lower courts. judicial decisions bind the parties directly involved, and may be appealed to in later similar cases as to any principle decided. all synods or councils, since the apostles’ times, whether general or particular, may err; and many have erred. therefore they are not to be made the rule of faith, or practice; but to be used as a help in both. the standards of review say plainly that scripture is the supreme judge, that this constitution is subordinate and fallible, and that it has nonetheless been adopted by the church. the purpose of the standards is to keep the constitution from being amended, violated or disregarded in judicial process.

title: Church Power and Its Limits
blurb: Power that is real, spiritual, joint when it judges, and only ministerial when it speaks.
text: church power and its limits power that is real, spiritual, joint when it judges, and only ministerial when it speaks. the power christ committed to his church vests in the whole body, rulers and ruled, which makes the church a spiritual commonwealth. as exercised by the people, that power extends to the choice of officers. officers exercise power in two ways. severally, in preaching, administering the sacraments, reproving the erring, visiting the sick and comforting the afflicted, which is the power of order. jointly, in church courts, after the form of judgment, which is the power of jurisdiction. an elder visiting a home is exercising the power of order. only a court can suspend anyone from the sacraments, receive a member, or judge a case. confusing the two is the most common error in practice. courts may frame symbols of faith, bear testimony against error in doctrine and immorality in practice, within or without the church, and decide cases of conscience. they may establish rules for government, discipline, worship and the church’s extension, which must agree with the doctrines of scripture, with only the circumstantial details left to christian prudence and wisdom. they may require obedience to the laws of christ, admitting the qualified and excluding the disobedient and disorderly. they may not make laws binding the conscience, and the highest censure their authority reaches is to cut off the contumacious and impenitent from the congregation of believers. there are some circumstances concerning the worship of god, and government of the church, common to human actions and societies, which are to be ordered by the light of nature, and christian prudence, according to the general rules of the word, which are always to be observed. the sole functions of the church, as a kingdom distinct from the civil commonwealth, are to proclaim, to administer and to enforce the law of christ revealed in scripture. the power of the church is exclusively spiritual; that of the state includes the exercise of force. the church has no right to construct or modify a government for the state, and the state has no right to frame a creed or polity for the church. church courts are altogether distinct from the civil magistracy, have no jurisdiction in political or civil affairs, and have no power to inflict temporal pains and penalties. where elders differ: this teaching is usually called the spirituality of the church, and its application is debated. the text itself both forbids jurisdiction in political and civil affairs and allows courts to bear testimony against immorality within or without the church. most disagreements are about where that line falls in a given year.

title: Vows, Subscription and Stated Differences
blurb: What an officer promises, what the church allows him to differ about, and how that difference is recorded.
text: vows, subscription and stated differences what an officer promises, what the church allows him to differ about, and how that difference is recorded. at ordination a minister answers questions put by the presiding minister, and a ruling elder or deacon answers a parallel set before the congregation. the wording is in the book at 21-5 and 24-6 and is not reproduced here. in substance, each officer affirms that the scriptures as originally given are the inerrant word of god and the only infallible rule of faith and practice; that he sincerely receives and adopts the confession and catechisms as containing the system of doctrine taught in scripture, and will on his own initiative make known any later change that puts him out of accord with a fundamental of that system; that he approves the form of government and discipline as conforming to the general principles of biblical polity; and that he promises subjection to his brethren in the lord. the minister also answers about his motives in seeking the office, his zeal for the truth and for the church’s purity, peace and unity under opposition, his faithfulness in all his duties, and his willingness to take charge of the particular church calling him. the congregation then answers its own questions, promising to receive the word from him, to submit to discipline duly exercised, to encourage him, and to maintain him. the constitution does not require a candidate to affirm every statement and proposition in the confession and catechisms. it is the right and responsibility of the presbytery to determine whether he is out of accord with any fundamental of those standards and so cannot in good faith receive and adopt them as containing the system of doctrine. the candidate must state the specific instances in which he differs. the court may grant an exception to a difference of doctrine only if in its judgment the difference is not out of accord with any fundamental of the system, because it is neither hostile to the system nor strikes at the vitals of religion. the same requirement follows a minister who transfers from another presbytery or another denomination. presbytery minutes record stated differences in the man’s own words, and record which of four findings the court made: that he stated no differences; that the difference is merely semantic; that it is more than semantic but not out of accord with any fundamental; or that it is out of accord, being hostile to the system or striking at the vitals of religion. the vow is not a one-time event. an officer promises to bring a later change of view to his court on his own initiative, and at ordination a man is asked whether his views have changed since he was licensed.

title: The Visible Church and the Particular Church
blurb: One church in every age, many congregations, and the jurisdiction lodged in each.
text: the visible church and the particular church one church in every age, many congregations, and the jurisdiction lodged in each. the church christ has erected in this world for the gathering and perfecting of the saints is his visible kingdom of grace, one and the same in all ages. its members are all those in every nation, together with their children, who profess faith in christ and promise submission to his laws. the visible church, which is also catholic or universal under the gospel (not confined to one nation, as before under the law), consists of all those throughout the world that profess the true religion; and of their children. division into denominations obscures the visible unity of the body but does not destroy it. those that maintain the word and sacraments in their fundamental integrity are to be recognised as true branches of the church of jesus christ. dividing into many individual churches follows scriptural example. the purest churches under heaven are subject both to mixture and error. a particular church is a number of professing christians, with their children, associated for divine worship and godly living according to the scriptures, and submitting to the lawful government of christ’s kingdom. its officers are its teaching and ruling elders and its deacons. its jurisdiction, being a joint power, is lodged in the session. the ordinances christ established in his church are prayer; singing praises; reading, expounding and preaching the word; the sacraments; public solemn fasting and thanksgiving; catechizing; offerings for the poor and other pious uses; the exercise of discipline; the taking of solemn vows; and ordination to sacred office. a church without a teaching elder is still to assemble. the session convenes the people on the lord’s day for prayer, praise, the reading and expounding of scripture, exhortation, or the reading of an approved sermon. a mission church answers the same description as a particular church, except that it has no permanent governing body and must be governed or supervised by others. its goal is to mature and be organised as a particular church as soon as that can be done in good order. its members are members of the presbyterian church in america, and it keeps its own rolls of communicant and non-communicant members.

title: Members: Children and Communicants
blurb: Two kinds of member, one covenant, and the vows by which a person enters.
text: members: children and communicants two kinds of member, one covenant, and the vows by which a person enters. the children of believers are, through the covenant and by right of birth, non-communing members of the church. they are entitled to baptism and to the pastoral oversight, instruction and government of the church, with a view to their embracing christ and possessing personally all the benefits of the covenant. communing members are those who have professed faith in christ, have been baptized, and have been admitted by the session to the lord’s table. only they are entitled to all the rights and privileges of the church, and only they vote. all baptized persons are entitled to the watchful care, instruction and government of the church, even adults who have made no profession of faith. no age is fixed for a covenant child’s profession. the time when young persons come to understand the gospel cannot be precisely set, and is left to the prudence of the session, whose office it is to judge the qualifications of those who apply, after careful examination. an unbaptized applicant, after satisfying the session as to knowledge and piety, ordinarily professes faith publicly and is then baptized. a baptized person admitted to the supper is encouraged to profess publicly, with clear recognition of the relation to the church he already had as a baptized member. those received by letter of transfer or by reaffirmation give a testimony of their christian experience to the session, and their names are announced to the congregation. in substance, a person making profession acknowledges himself a sinner in the sight of god, justly deserving his displeasure and without hope except in sovereign mercy; believes in jesus christ as the son of god and savior of sinners, receiving and resting on him alone for salvation as he is offered in the gospel; resolves and promises, relying on the grace of the holy spirit, to live as a follower of christ; promises to support the church in its worship and work to the best of his ability; and submits to the government and discipline of the church, promising to study its purity and peace. the book calls these declarations and promises a solemn covenant with god and his church. two later provisions lean on them: erasure for willful neglect points back to vows three to five, and every disciplinary case rests on the fact that a member has submitted to the church’s government. all baptized persons are subject to the discipline of the church and entitled to its benefits. the nurture of covenant children belongs first to parents, who are responsible to the church for it, and the session is to establish and control sunday schools and bible classes with special reference to the children of the church. adult non-communing members who receive the church’s oversight with meekness are entitled to special attention: their rights and privileges under the covenant should be explained frequently and fully, and they should be warned of the danger of neglecting covenant obligations.

title: Transfers, Withdrawal and Erasure
blurb: How names come off a roll, and the difference between pastoral removal and censure.
text: transfers, withdrawal and erasure how names come off a roll, and the difference between pastoral removal and censure. a member who moves beyond the bounds of his congregation, so that he can no longer attend its services regularly, has the duty to transfer his membership by a certificate of dismission. where no session exists or a certificate cannot be had, another church’s session may receive him on other satisfactory testimonials and must notify his former church. the elders of the church he has left are to continue pastoral oversight as far as possible, to tell him of his duty to transfer, and to ask the elders where he now lives to take oversight of him. if after being advised he neglects for one year to transfer, the session proceeds under 38-4, with allowance for special cases such as servicemen and students. a member remains under the jurisdiction of the dismissing session until he is actually received elsewhere, and a certificate of dismission is good testimony of standing for one year. if a member or officer in good standing joins another branch of the visible church, the irregularity is recorded, the new membership acknowledged, and the name removed. if an investigation or charges are pending, the court of original jurisdiction may keep his name on the roll and conduct the case, or may let him go and, on request, communicate the matters to the receiving body. if the body he joins is judged by his court to fail to maintain the word and sacraments in their fundamental integrity, he is to be warned of his danger. if he persists, his name is erased, and if he is an officer, the authority to exercise his office as derived from this church is withdrawn. where a member has willfully neglected the church for a year, or has made known that he does not intend to keep his vows, the session continues pastoral discipline in the spirit of galatians 6:1. it reminds him, if possible in person and in writing, of the promises by which he entered a solemn covenant with god and his church, and warns him that his name will be erased if he persists. after diligent pastoral work, further inquiry and due delay, if the session judges that he will not fulfil his obligations in this or any other branch of the visible church, it erases his name and notifies him if possible. if the member asks in writing for process, the session must grant it. erasure is an act of pastoral discipline without process. it is not excommunication, which is a censure imposed after trial on an offender who is incorrigible and contumacious. a presbytery dissolving a church gives at least sixty days notice and tells the members of their responsibility to transfer. it may transfer members with their consent and the consent of receiving sessions, grant letters of dismissal testifying to good standing at the date of dissolution, or place members under a commission acting as a session for up to a year, renewable.

title: Offices: Elders and Deacons
blurb: Which offices continue, how they are classed, and who may hold them.
text: offices: elders and deacons which offices continue, how they are classed, and who may hold them. under the new testament our lord first gathered his people through extraordinary officers who received extraordinary gifts of the spirit and were agents by whom god completed his revelation. such officers and gifts, tied as they were to new revelation, have no successors, since revelation was completed at the close of the apostolic age. the ordinary and perpetual classes of office are elders and deacons. within the class of elder are the two orders of teaching elder and ruling elder. the elders jointly have the government and spiritual oversight of the church, including teaching, and only those elders specially gifted, called and trained by god to preach may serve as teaching elders. the office of deacon is not one of rule but of service, to the physical and spiritual needs of the people. in accord with scripture these offices are open to men only. bishop, pastor, presbyter, elder and teacher are titles that express the various duties of one and the same office. they do not indicate grades. ruling elders possess the same authority and eligibility to office in the courts of the church as teaching elders, and should cultivate their own aptness to teach the bible and use every opportunity to do so. this is why every court is in nature a presbytery: each is composed exclusively of presbyters. no officeholder may usurp authority in the church or receive official titles of spiritual pre-eminence except those scripture employs. unordained people are not to be referred to as, or given the titles of, the ordained offices of pastor, elder or deacon. it is often expedient for a session to select and appoint godly men and women of the congregation to assist the deacons in caring for the sick, widows, orphans, prisoners and others in distress or need. these assistants are not officers of the church and are not subjects for ordination. where elders differ: some describe this arrangement as two offices with two orders of elder, others speak of three offices, distinguishing the minister from the ruling elder. debate also continues over how far 9-7 reaches and what titles 7-3 permits for staff. the text itself sets two classes, two orders within the first, and one rule about titles.

title: The Elder
blurb: Qualifications, duties, and what is added when an elder is called to preach.
text: the elder qualifications, duties, and what is added when an elder is called to preach. the office is one of dignity and usefulness. the man who fills it should possess a competency of human learning, be blameless in life, sound in the faith and apt to teach; should show a sobriety and holiness of life becoming the gospel; should conform to the biblical requirement of chastity and sexual purity in his descriptions of himself and in his convictions, character and conduct; the chair to rule that something now happening is out of order. it does not require a second and it interrupts, because it concerns the conduct of business rather than its substance. the chair rules, and states the reason for the ruling. an appeal from the decision of the chair takes that ruling to the body itself, which decides by vote whether the chair’s ruling stands. between them, these two motions mean that no moderator has the last word on his own rulings. these are the two devices a member reaches for when a meeting is going wrong. learning them is worth more than learning the whole table of motions, because everything else can wait for the next meeting and these cannot. the assembly’s guidelines for the minutes of a presbytery state the reason plainly. points of order ruled against by the chair, and appeals from the decision of the chair, whether sustained or lost, together with the reason the chair gave for his ruling, should be entered in the minutes for the sake of any case that may be carried to a higher court, and for the protection of a minority. that single rule ties this unit to the rest of the course. a higher court reviewing a lower one asks whether the proceedings were correctly recorded, whether they were regular and constitutional, whether they were wise and equitable, and whether its own lawful injunctions were obeyed. an appeal is heard on the record of the case and on nothing outside it. a ruling that was never written down cannot be reviewed, and a member who was overruled has nothing to show. the same instinct runs through the filing periods for a dissent, a protest or an objection: thirty days to put a position on the record, or before the assembly adjourns. presentations informing the assembly of the work reported by permanent committees and agencies are limited to fifteen minutes. budgets agreed upon by the administrative committee may be changed only by a two-thirds vote of commissioners present and voting, and that threshold applies only to changes initiated on the floor. on a question of direct personal interest, commissioners are pointed to the standard manual's counsel on abstaining. in the overtures committee no motion to limit or extend the limits of debate is permitted, and the previous question carries on three-fourths of the members present and voting.

title: Candidates and Licensure
blurb: Coming under care, and the licence that lets a man preach before he is ordained.
text: candidates and licensure coming under care, and the licence that lets a man preach before he is ordained. a candidate for the ministry is a member of the church in full communion who, believing himself called to preach, submits himself to the care and guidance of a presbytery during his course of study and practical training. every applicant puts himself under the care of a presbytery, ordinarily the one with jurisdiction over the church of which he is a member. his session’s endorsement must be given, with testimonials of his christian character and promise of usefulness, and should describe the ministry he has taken part in, with a brief evaluation. he must have been a member of the endorsing congregation for at least six months before filing, except where presbytery deems the case extraordinary. a man may not be received under care and examined for ordination at the same meeting, since he must serve at least a year of internship before ordination. he may, however, be taken under care, licensed to preach and made an intern at the same meeting. the applicant appears in person and is examined on experiential religion and on his motives for seeking the ministry. if the testimonials and examination are satisfactory, he answers two questions, promising to maintain a becoming christian character and to be diligent in preparation, and to submit to the proper supervision of presbytery in matters concerning that preparation. he is then given a charge, and his name is placed on the roll of candidates. a candidate remains a private member of his church under the session’s jurisdiction, while his preparation is under the oversight of presbytery. presbytery owes him kindly interest, counsel and guidance about studies and training, and no candidate may omit any subject prescribed as a test for ordination without presbytery’s consent, which must be recorded with its reasons. he reports to presbytery at least once a year, and presbytery secures an annual report from his instructors on deportment, diligence and progress. he may be dismissed to another presbytery, may withdraw at his own or his session’s request, and may have his name removed by presbytery for sufficient reasons, which must be recorded and reported to him and his session. to preserve the purity of preaching, no man may preach regularly in pca pulpits without proper licensure from the presbytery with jurisdiction where he will preach. a ruling elder, a candidate, a minister of another denomination or another man may be licensed on giving satisfaction as to his gifts and passing the examination. the examination covers a statement of his christian experience and inward call, written or oral at presbytery’s discretion; his basic knowledge of biblical doctrine as outlined in the confession and catechisms; his practical knowledge of bible content; his basic knowledge of the government of this church as defined in the book of church order; oral examination on those views; and a written sermon on an assigned passage, presented orally to presbytery or a committee. as at ordination, the applicant must state the specific instances in which he differs with the confession and catechisms, and an exception may be granted only where the difference is neither hostile to the system nor strikes at the vitals of religion. no part of the examination is omitted except in extraordinary cases, and then the reasons and the omitted parts are recorded. the licentiate answers four questions: on the scriptures as the inerrant word and only infallible rule; on receiving and adopting the confession and catechisms as containing the system of doctrine; on striving for the purity, peace, unity and edification of the church; and on submitting himself, in the lord, to the government of that presbytery or of any other into whose bounds he may be called. a licence expires after four years and may be renewed without further examination if presbytery thinks proper, but the licentiate must apply before it expires. i

title: Internship and the Call
blurb: A year of tested work, then a call to definite labour before any man is ordained.
text: internship and the call a year of tested work, then a call to definite labour before any man is ordained. scripture requires that trial be made of those who are to be ordained, both as to their gifts and as to their ability to rule as teaching elders, so that the office is not degraded and the church can form a better judgment. to provide that trial, a candidate for ordination must serve an internship of at least one year, longer at presbytery’s discretion. the internship may fall during or after formal theological education, and may run alongside academic work. its nature is determined by presbytery, but it should involve the man in the full scope of the duties of a regular ministerial calling, and it is both practical instruction and testing, under close supervision. an intern may chair a session meeting temporarily if the moderator asks him to, under supervision and subject to being overruled. he is not a member of the session and does not vote unless he has already been ordained a ruling elder and elected to it. he has the right to conduct funerals. he may not administer the sacraments. at the end of the period set, the internship is approved or disapproved. even when approved, the man cannot be ordained without a call to specific work. if it is disapproved, presbytery may extend it or rescind his intern status. presbytery may also approve previous equivalent experience by a three-fourths vote at a regular meeting, once its committee reports at least a year of comparable ministry, satisfactory performance of the full scope of ministerial duties, and the manifest approbation of god’s people in a local church. before a candidate or licentiate can be ordained he must receive a call to a definite work, ordinarily from a church, a presbytery or the general assembly of this denomination. if the call comes from another source, presbytery records why it considers the work a valid christian ministry. a proper call must be in writing and in the hands of presbytery before it acts. it must include the financial arrangements, such as salary, vacation, insurance and retirement, and an assurance that the work will afford liberty to proclaim and practise fully and freely the whole counsel of god as contained in scripture and understood in the westminster confession. every church should be under the pastoral oversight of a minister, and a church without a pastor should seek one without delay. the session calls a congregational meeting to elect a pulpit committee, which may be drawn from the congregation at large or from the session as the congregation designates. after consultation the committee recommends a candidate who in its judgment meets the constitutional requirements of the office and is best suited to the congregation’s spiritual interests. the session orders a congregational meeting at the regular place of worship, with public notice of time, place and purpose at least one week beforehand. the congregation should elect a minister or ruling elder of this church to preside if that is practicable, and otherwise any male member of the church. all communing members in good and regular standing, and no others, may vote, and a majority of votes cast, excluding blanks and abstentions, elects. if a large minority is averse to the man who received a majority and cannot be brought to concur, the moderator endeavors to dissuade the majority from prosecuting the call. if the electors are nearly unanimous, or the majority insists on its right, the moderator draws the call in due form, certifies in writing the number who did not concur and any facts of importance, and lays all of it before presbytery with the call. the call itself follows the form in the book: the congregation declares itself satisfied of the man’s ministerial qualifications, promises him support, encouragement and obedience in the lord, and obliges itself to the stated maintenance. commissioners appointed by the church present and prosecute the call before presbytery, which ma

title: Ordination Trials and Installation
blurb: The examinations that stand between a call and the laying on of hands.
text: ordination trials and installation the examinations that stand between a call and the laying on of hands. no minister, licentiate or candidate receives a call from a church except by permission of his presbytery. when a call is presented and found in order, and presbytery deems it for the good of the church, the call is placed in the man’s hands. ordinarily a man does not move to the field before his examination for licensure or ordination, and an ordained man coming from another presbytery or denomination ordinarily does not move before he is examined and received. an intern who has completed his internship to presbytery’s satisfaction and accepted a call is to be ordained without delay. no presbytery ordains a man to labour within the bounds of another presbytery; it furnishes testimonials and sends him to submit himself to the presbytery where he expects to work. an intern applying for ordination presents a diploma from an approved college or university and from an approved theological seminary, or authentic testimonials of a completed course of theological studies, or a certificate from a theological study programme approved by the assembly and one of the presbyteries. these educational requirements are omitted only in extraordinary cases, and then only by a three-fourths vote, with reasons recorded. he also presents testimonials of a completed and approved internship. a careful examination on his acquaintance with experiential religion, especially personal character and family management, on the qualifications of 1 timothy 3 and titus 1. his knowledge of the greek and hebrew languages. a presbytery may accept a seminary degree that includes study in the original languages in place of an oral examination in them. bible content, theology, the sacraments, church history, the history of this church, and the principles and rules of its government and discipline. a thesis on a theological topic assigned by presbytery. an exegesis on an assigned portion of scripture, requiring the use of the original languages. a sermon preached before presbytery or a committee of it. no part of the trials is omitted except in extraordinary cases, and then only by a three-fourths approval, with the reasons and the omitted parts recorded. the book warns that these extraordinary clauses are meant for extraordinary circumstances of the church or proven extraordinary gifts of the man, and that presbyteries must neither block a genuinely exceptional candidate nor ordain a man who is inadequately prepared. in examining character, presbytery gives specific attention to potential notorious concerns and careful attention to the man’s practical struggle against sinful actions and persistent sinful desires, and requires clear testimony of reliance on union with christ for progress over sin and for fruit. the same paragraph warns against confessing sins publicly in a way that makes them seem matters of little consequence. the constitution does not require affirmation of every proposition in the standards, and the presbytery judges any stated difference by the test described in the lesson on subscription. on the day appointed, ordinarily in the church he is to serve, a sermon is preached, the presiding member recites the proceedings, and the candidate answers the ordination questions. the congregation then answers four questions of its own, professing readiness to receive him, promising to receive the word from him with meekness and love and to submit to him in the due exercise of discipline, to encourage him, and to continue the maintenance promised. he kneels, and with prayer and the laying on of the hands of the presbytery he is solemnly set apart. the members give him the right hand of fellowship, the presiding minister declares him regularly elected, ordained and installed, and a charge is given to pastor and congregation. for an assistant pastor only the first seven questions are used, the session is addressed instead of the congregation, and the word

title: Pastoral Relations and Their End
blurb: Pastor, associate and assistant, temporary supplies, and how a pastoral relation is dissolved.
text: pastoral relations and their end pastor, associate and assistant, temporary supplies, and how a pastoral relation is dissolved. the pastoral relations are pastor, associate pastor and assistant pastor. the pastor and associate pastor are elected by the congregation using the form of call, and because they are elected by the congregation they are members of the session. an existing assistant pastor may be elected associate pastor on the session’s recommendation, without the election of a pulpit committee. an assistant pastor is called by the session with the permission and approval of presbytery. he is not a member of the session, though he may be appointed on special occasions to moderate it. the relationship of an associate pastor to the church is determined by the congregation; that of an assistant pastor is determined by the session. dissolution of either is governed by chapter 23. where changes in a pastorate require it, a temporary relation may be established with a minister called a stated supply. where no pastor or stated supply can be secured, the session with presbytery’s approval may establish a temporary relation with a licentiate as student supply, or with a ruling elder supply. such relations run no longer than one year, renewable at the session’s request and on presbytery’s review. when a minister tenders his resignation to presbytery, the presbytery cites the church to appear by its commissioners and show cause why the resignation should or should not be accepted. if the church fails to appear, or if its reasons are deemed insufficient, the resignation is accepted and the relation dissolved. where a church wishes to be relieved of its pastor, the same procedure is followed. whichever party begins, there is always a congregational meeting, called and conducted in the same manner as the call of a pastor. the minister must not physically leave the field until presbytery, or a commission empowered to handle uncontested requests, has dissolved the relation. associate and assistant pastors may continue when the senior pastor’s relation is dissolved, but they may not normally succeed him without an intervening term of service in a different field. a congregation may petition presbytery for an exception by a four-fifths majority on secret ballot, and presbytery may grant it by a three-fourths majority. presbytery is to determine whether the dissolution of the senior pastor’s relationship was brought about in christian love and good order on the part of those concerned. presbytery may designate a minister honorably retired when he wishes to retire by reason of age, or medically disabled when infirmity has ended his active ministry. in either case he continues to hold membership in his presbytery and may serve on committees or commissions if elected or appointed. a congregation that wishes to honour his past labours among them may elect him pastor emeritus.

title: Congregational Meetings
blurb: What a congregation may decide, how a meeting is called, and what makes it valid.
text: congregational meetings what a congregation may decide, how a meeting is called, and what makes it valid. the congregation consists of all the communing members of a particular church, and they only are entitled to vote. its distinctive acts are few and weighty: it elects ruling elders and deacons, elects a pulpit committee, calls a pastor, acts on its property through trustees or corporation officers, and may ask the session to release an officer. whenever it seems for the best interests of the church, the session calls a congregational meeting and gives public notice of at least one week. no business is transacted except what the notice states. the session must always call a meeting when asked in writing by a set proportion of the communing members: a fourth in a church of not more than 100; a fifth in a church of more than 100 and not more than 300; a sixth in a church of more than 300 and not more than 500; a seventh in a church of more than 500 and not more than 700; and 100 members in a church of more than 700. if on a proper request the session cannot act, fails to act or refuses to act within thirty days, any member or members in good standing may file a complaint. the quorum is a fourth of the resident communing members in a church of not more than 100, and a sixth of them in a larger church. the pastor is moderator of congregational meetings by virtue of his office. if it is impracticable or inexpedient for him to preside, or there is no pastor, the session appoints one of its number to call the meeting to order and preside until the congregation elects its presiding officer, who may be a minister or ruling elder of this church, or any male member of that particular church. a clerk is elected to serve for that meeting or a definite period. he keeps correct minutes of the proceedings and business, preserves them in permanent form after they are attested by the moderator and the clerk, and sends a copy to the session. a congregational meeting is not a court. it does not judge cases, receive members, or discipline anyone. those acts belong to the session, and the congregation’s remedy against a session’s act is a complaint, not a vote. the notice defines the business. a meeting properly called to elect officers cannot be turned into a meeting about the budget or the building.

title: Property and the Freedom to Withdraw
blurb: The chapter that decides who owns the building, and what a congregation may do with it.
text: property and the freedom to withdraw the chapter that decides who owns the building, and what a congregation may do with it. an unincorporated church may elect trustees with power to buy, sell or mortgage property, to accept and execute deeds, to hold and defend title, and to manage permanent special funds. such trustees act solely under the instructions of the congregation and may not infringe on the powers of the session or the board of deacons. where a church is incorporated, its charter and bylaws must always accord with the constitution of this church. all communing members on the roll are members of the corporation, and its officers are elected from among them in a regularly constituted congregational meeting. funds collected for the support and expenses of the church and for its benevolences are controlled and disbursed by the session and the board of deacons as their authorities are defined. the corporation, through its trustees or officers, or in an unincorporated church those entitled to represent it in matters of real property, has sole title to its property, real, personal or mixed, tangible or intangible, and is sole owner of any equity in real estate or of any fund or property held by or belonging to the church or any group within it. the higher courts may receive money or property from a local church only by its free and voluntary action. all particular churches are entitled to hold, own and enjoy their own local properties, without any right of reversion whatsoever to any presbytery, general assembly or any court hereafter created, or to the trustees or officers of such courts. the provisions of chapter 25 are to be construed as a solemn covenant by which the church as a whole promises never to attempt to secure possession of the property of any congregation against its will, whether or not the congregation stays in this body, and all officers and courts are forbidden to make such an attempt. a particular church need remain in association with any court of this body only so long as it desires. the relationship is voluntary, based on mutual love and confidence, and is in no sense maintained by force or coercion. a church may withdraw at any time for reasons that seem sufficient to it, provided the congregation is given at least thirty days notice of the meeting at which the withdrawal is to be voted. if a church is dissolved by presbytery at the congregation’s request and no disposition of its property has been made within six months, those who held title deliver and convey it to the presbytery, which applies the property or its proceeds at its discretion. in the presbyterian church (u.s.a.) all property held by or for a congregation is held in trust for that denomination, and the relationship of a congregation to the denomination may be severed only by constitutional action on the part of the presbytery. the pca’s book takes the opposite path on both points. this is one of the sharpest practical differences between american presbyterian bodies, and it explains much of the property litigation of the last century. it also explains why the pca’s founding congregations could leave with their buildings.

title: Planting and Organizing a Church
blurb: How a mission church is begun, governed for a time, and constituted as a particular church.
text: planting and organizing a church how a mission church is begun, governed for a time, and constituted as a particular church. mission churches are ordinarily established by presbyteries within their bounds. a presbytery may act on its own initiative, respond to the initiative of a session, or answer the written petition of an independent gathering of believers who wish to become a congregation. where an existing non-pca church wishes to come in, presbytery works with its leadership to decide whether it should enter as a mission church or seek reception under 13-8. if a mission church lies outside the bounds of a presbytery, responsibility may be exercised through the assembly’s committee on mission to north america or mission to the world, which then exercises the powers given to presbytery in these provisions. should it become necessary, presbytery may dissolve a mission church, caring for its members by the procedures used when a church is dissolved. because of its transitional condition, a mission church needs a temporary system of government. at its discretion presbytery may appoint an evangelist, may cooperate with the session of a particular church in a mother and daughter relationship so that the session serves as the temporary governing body, or may appoint a commission to serve as a temporary session, in which case a minister approved to serve as pastor is included and serves as moderator. the temporary government records its acts and submits its records to presbytery for annual review like any session. pastoral ministry may be provided by a minister called by presbytery to serve as pastor, by stated, student or ruling elder supply, or by a series of qualified preachers approved by the temporary government. the temporary government receives members under the provisions of chapter 57 so far as they apply, and those received are communing or non-communing members of the presbyterian church in america. mission churches have the right of judicial process to the court overseeing their temporary government. a new church can be organised only by the authority of presbytery. a presbytery should have standing rules setting the prerequisites that qualify a mission church to begin the process, such as the minimum number of petitioners and the level of financial support, and the number of officers sufficient for a session quorum is necessary to complete it. the temporary government oversees the steps and, when men appear qualified, begins the nomination and election process under chapter 24 so far as it applies. elections normally take place at least two weeks before the organization service, though the new officers take office at the completion of that service. if no deacons are elected, their duties fall to the session until deacons can be secured. where a minister approved to serve as pastor is in place and members have been received, the temporary session may call a congregational meeting at which the congregation may call him as pastor by majority vote without the steps of chapter 20. otherwise a pastor is called under chapter 20 so far as it applies. the members sign a petition to presbytery asking to be organised, and on approval presbytery appoints an organizing commission and sets the date and time of the service. at the service the commission ordains and installs the officers, ordains or installs a pastor where that is part of the service, asks the communicant members present to enter into covenant by answering a question with uplifted hand, promising to walk together as a particular church on the principles of the faith and order of this church and to be zealous and faithful in maintaining the purity and peace of the whole body, and then declares them constituted a church according to the word of god. once organised, the new session should meet as soon as practicable to elect a stated clerk and form a budget. if there is no pastor, the session may elect a moderator from its own number or any teaching elder of presbytery

title: What Discipline Is For
blurb: Two senses of the word, three ends, and the order the steps must follow.
text: what discipline is for two senses of the word, three ends, and the order the steps must follow. discipline is the exercise of authority given the church by the lord jesus christ to instruct and guide its members and to promote its purity and welfare. the term has two senses: the whole government, inspection, training, guardianship and control the church maintains over its members, officers and courts; and a restricted, technical sense meaning judicial process. all baptized persons, being members of the church, are subject to its discipline and entitled to its benefits. discipline maintains the glory of god, the purity of his church, and the keeping and reclaiming of disobedient sinners. so far as it involves judicial action, its ends are the rebuke of offenses, the removal of scandal, the vindication of the honour of christ, the promotion of the purity and general edification of the church, and the spiritual good of offenders themselves. the power christ has given the church is for building up and not for destruction, and is exercised under a dispensation of mercy rather than of wrath. as in preaching the wicked are doctrinally separated from the good, so by discipline the church authoritatively separates between the holy and the profane, acting the part of a tender mother correcting her children for their good. church censures are necessary, for the reclaiming and gaining of offending brethren, for deterring of others from the like offenses, for purging out of that leaven which might infect the whole lump, for vindicating the honor of christ, and the holy profession of the gospel, and for preventing the wrath of god. scriptural law is the basis of all discipline because it is the revelation of god’s holy will. the proper principles are instruction in the word; the responsibility of individuals to admonish one another; if admonition is rejected, the calling of one or more witnesses; and if rejection persists, action by the church through her court unto admonition, suspension, excommunication and deposition. these steps must be followed in proper order. teaching elders are charged to instruct the officers in discipline, to instruct the congregation in discipline, and to practise it jointly in the context of the congregation and the church courts. discipline that is unknown until it is used will always look arbitrary. the spiritual nurture, instruction and training of the children of the church are committed by god primarily to their parents, who are responsible to the church for the discharge of their obligations. the church should maintain constant and sympathetic relations with the children, encourage them, when they come to years of discretion, to confess christ and seek admission to the lord’s supper, and where they are wayward should cherish them and use every means to reclaim them.

title: Offenses and Censures
blurb: What may be charged, and the five censures a court may impose.
text: offenses and censures what may be charged, and the five censures a court may impose. an offense, the proper object of judicial process, is anything in the doctrines or practice of a church member professing faith in christ that is contrary to the word of god. the confession and catechisms, with the formularies of government, discipline and worship, are accepted as standard expositions of the teachings of scripture in relation to faith and practice. nothing may be considered an offense, or admitted as a matter of accusation, which cannot be proved to be such from scripture as interpreted in these standards. offenses are personal or general, private or public, and all of them, being sins against god, are grounds of discipline. personal offenses are violations of divine law considered as wrongs or injuries to particular individuals; general offenses are heresies or immoralities having no such relation, or considered apart from it. private offenses are known only to a few; public offenses are notorious. personal and private are not synonyms, and the pair of distinctions matters in practice. whether an offense is personal decides whether the matthew 18 steps must come first. whether it is public shapes how the censure is administered. admonition: the formal reproof of an offender by a court, warning him of his guilt and danger and exhorting him to be more circumspect and watchful. suspension from the sacraments: temporary exclusion from them, always indefinite as to duration. there is no definite suspension from the sacraments. suspension from office: the exclusion of an officer from his office, which may be definite or indefinite. excommunication: the excision of an offender from the communion of the church, inflicted only for gross crime or heresy where the offender shows himself incorrigible and contumacious. deposition: the degradation of an officer from his office, which may or may not be accompanied by other censure. admonition or definite suspension from office is administered to a convicted person who satisfies the court as to his repentance and makes appropriate restitution, and such a censure concludes the judicial process. indefinite suspension or excommunication is administered to one who, upon conviction, remains impenitent. for officers, suspension from the sacraments always carries suspension from office with it, though suspension from office does not always carry suspension from the sacraments. definite suspension from office is used where the credit of religion, the honour of christ and the good of the delinquent require it, even though he has satisfied the court. censures and the modes of administering them are suited to the nature of the offense. for private offenses, censure is administered in the presence of the court alone, or privately by one or more of its members. for public offenses, the degree and the mode lie within the court’s discretion, following the paragraphs that deal with particular censures. the book supplies the words for each sentence, to be spoken by the moderator: for definite suspension from office, for indefinite suspension, for excommunication and for deposition. the forms for definite and indefinite suspension were revised in 2026.

title: Parties, Charges and Trial
blurb: Who prosecutes, what must be in writing, and the order a trial follows.
text: parties, charges and trial who prosecutes, what must be in writing, and the order a trial follows. it is the duty of sessions and presbyteries to exercise care over those under their authority, and with due diligence and great discretion to require satisfactory explanations concerning reports affecting a person’s christian character. that duty is more imperative where a person who believes himself wronged by injurious reports asks for an investigation. if the investigation raises a strong presumption of guilt, the court institutes process and appoints a prosecutor to prepare the indictment and conduct the case. the original and only parties in a case of process are the accuser and the accused, and the accuser is always the presbyterian church in america, whose honour and purity are to be maintained. the prosecutor, voluntary or appointed, always represents the church. every indictment begins in the name of this church and concludes against the peace, unity and purity of the church and the honour and majesty of the lord jesus christ as its king and head. an injured party may not become the prosecutor of a personal offense without first trying the means of reconciliation and of reclaiming the offender that christ requires. a court may still investigate a personal offense as if it were general where the interest of religion seems to demand it. great caution is to be used in receiving accusations from a person known to indulge a malignant spirit, of poor character, himself under censure, deeply interested in a conviction, or known to be litigious, rash or highly imprudent. a voluntary prosecutor is warned beforehand that if he fails to show probable cause he may himself be censured as a slanderer of the brethren. when a member of a court is under process, all his official functions may be administratively suspended at the court’s discretion. this is never done by way of censure, and it requires a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, abstentions not counted, at the meeting of the session or presbytery, even where a commission is conducting the process. that requirement was amended in 2026. in discussion of questions in his own case, the accused has the rights of a defendant only, not of a judge. process is not commenced unless some person undertakes to make out the charge, or the court finds it necessary for the honour of religion to act itself. when a charge is laid before a session or presbytery it is reduced to writing, and nothing is done at the first meeting, except by consent of parties, but three things: appointing a prosecutor; ordering the indictment drawn and a copy served on the accused with the names of known witnesses; and citing the accused to appear at another meeting not sooner than ten days later. at that second meeting the charges are read to the accused and he is called on to plead. if he confesses, the court may deal with him at its discretion. if he pleads and takes issue, the trial is scheduled and the parties and witnesses cited, and the trial is not sooner than fourteen days after that citation. in drawing the indictment the times, places and circumstances should be stated particularly, so that the accused can make his defense. an accused who refuses to obey a citation is cited a second time with notice that he will be dealt with for contumacy if he does not appear. one who appears and refuses to plead, or otherwise refuses to cooperate with lawful proceedings, is likewise dealt with for contumacy. it is appropriate that with each citation the moderator or clerk draw the parties’ attention to the rules of discipline and help them obtain access to them. when the trial is about to begin, the moderator announces from the chair that the court is passing to the consideration of the case, and charges the members to remember their character as judges of a court of jesus christ. witnesses are examined in the presence of the accused, or at least after due citation, and may be cross-examined by both part

title: Members, Ministers and Evidence
blurb: The special rules for Sessions and for ministers, and the law of proof.
