title: How Higher Courts Review Lower Courts
blurb: Four modes of supervision, the annual reading of records, and the four standards of review.
text: how higher courts review lower courts four modes of supervision, the annual reading of records, and the four standards of review. the acts and decisions of a lower court come under the supervision of a higher court in one of four ways: review and control, reference, appeal and complaint. when the proceedings of a lower court are before a higher court, the members of the lower court keep their right to sit, deliberate and vote, except in cases of appeal or complaint. it is the right and duty of every court above the session to review, at least once a year, the records of the court next below. if a lower court fails to present its records, the higher court may require them immediately or at a time it fixes. whether the proceedings have been correctly recorded. whether they have been regular and in accordance with the constitution. whether they have been wise, equitable and suited to promote the welfare of the church. whether the lawful injunctions of the higher court have been obeyed. ordinarily the higher court simply records whether it approves, disapproves or corrects the records in any particular. where a serious irregularity appears, it may require review and correction by the lower court. proceedings in judicial cases are not dealt with under review and control once notice of appeal or complaint has been given, and no judgment in a judicial case is reversed except by appeal or complaint. courts sometimes neglect their duty altogether, so that heretical opinions or corrupt practices gain ground, gross offenders escape, or irregular proceedings go unrecorded. where the next higher court is well advised of such neglect or irregularity, it must take cognizance of the matter and examine, deliberate and judge as completely as if it had come up by review of records. where a court with appellate jurisdiction receives a credible report of important delinquency or grossly unconstitutional proceedings in the court below, the first step is to cite that court to appear, by representative or in writing, at a specified time and place, and to show what it has done or failed to do. the citing court may then reverse or redress the proceedings in other than judicial cases, censure the delinquent court, remit the matter with an injunction to dispose of it constitutionally, or stay further proceedings. the constitution is fallible and subordinate to scripture, and it has been adopted by the church as a standard exposition of scripture’s teaching. to keep it from being amended, violated or disregarded in judicial process, any review of the judicial proceedings of a lower court is guided by four principles. the higher court limits itself to the issues raised by the parties in the original court, and resolves them by applying the constitution as established through the constitutional process. it ordinarily shows great deference to the lower court on factual matters the lower court is more competent to determine, because of its proximity to events and its personal knowledge of the parties and witnesses, and does not reverse a factual finding unless there is clear error. it shows the same deference on matters of discretion and judgment that only a court with familiar acquaintance of the events and parties can address, such as the moral character of candidates for office, the appropriate censure after a trial, or the comparative credibility of conflicting witnesses, and does not reverse unless there is clear error. it owes no such deference on the interpretation of the constitution, where it has the duty and authority to interpret and apply according to its best ability and understanding, whatever the lower court's opinion. read together, these four sentences explain most outcomes on appeal. a party who wants a factual finding reversed must show clear error. a party arguing that the lower court misread the constitution is not asking for deference at all.

title: References, Appeals and Complaints
blurb: Three named routes upward, and how to tell which one a case needs.
text: references, appeals and complaints three named routes upward, and how to tell which one a case needs. a reference is a written representation and application made by a lower court to a higher one for advice or other action on a matter still pending below, ordinarily to the next higher court. proper subjects are matters that are new, delicate or difficult, or on which the members are seriously divided, or which involve the constitution and legal procedures where the lower court feels the need of guidance. a lower court may ask for advice only, or for final disposition. in particular it may refer a judicial case with a request that the higher court take original jurisdiction of the case, its trial, judgment and whatever censure it deems warranted; or that the higher court provide additional teaching and ruling elders to serve with the lower court in the case, who during their service have all the rights and responsibilities of judges there, subject to the parties’ right of challenge. that provision was amended in 2026. although references are sometimes proper, in general it is better that every court discharge the duty assigned it under the law of the church. a higher court is not required to accede, but should ordinarily give advice when it is requested. an appeal is the transfer to a higher court of a judicial case on which judgment has been rendered below, and is allowable only to the party against whom the decision was rendered. it cannot be taken to any court other than the next higher, except with that court’s consent. those entitled to appeal are those who have submitted to a regular trial, those appealing a censure in a case without process, those appealing the raising of a censure under 36-8, and those appealing a divestiture without censure under 34-10. the grounds are such as these: irregularity in the proceedings of the lower court; refusal of reasonable indulgence to a party on trial; receiving improper evidence or declining to receive proper evidence; hurrying to a decision before all the testimony is taken; manifestation of prejudice in the case; and mistake or injustice in the judgment and censure. notice of appeal may be given before the court adjourns, and written notice with supporting reasons must be filed with the clerk of the lower court and the clerk of the higher court within thirty days of notification of the decision. the clerk of the lower court files the record of the case with the higher court within thirty days of receiving notice. notice of appeal suspends the judgment until the case is decided, though the court of original jurisdiction may, for recorded reasons, keep the appellant from the lord’s table or from some or all official functions, never as censure and only by a two-thirds majority. at the hearing, after the record is read, each side has not over thirty minutes for oral argument, the appellant opening and closing. the court or commission then goes into closed session and votes on each specification of error in the form: shall this specification of error be sustained. the decision may affirm in whole or part, reverse in whole or part, render the decision that should have been rendered, or remand for a new trial, and a written opinion is always prepared. an appellant who fails to appear is considered to have abandoned his appeal, and one who manifests a litigious or otherwise unchristian spirit receives a suitable rebuke. a complaint is a written representation made against some act or decision of a court. any communing member of the church in good standing may complain against any action of a court to whose jurisdiction he is subject, except that no complaint is allowable in a judicial case after process has commenced. where such a complaint is timely filed after process has begun, its adjudication waits until the judicial case is complete or any appeal is finished or withdrawn. that provision was amended in 2025. a complaint is made first to the court whose act is alleged to be in error,

blurb: What the Directory is, what it binds, and the elements it names.
text: principles of worship and the lord’s day what the directory is, what it binds, and the elements it names. a statement adopted by the third general assembly prefaces the directory: it is an later given full constitutional authority after two-thirds of the presbyteries approved, and section 59-3 was given the same authority in the same way. since the holy scriptures are the only infallible rule of faith and practice, the principles of public worship must be derived from the bible and from no other source. scripture forbids worshipping god by images or in any way not appointed in his word, and requires the receiving, observing and keeping pure and entire all such religious worship and ordinances as god has appointed. the acceptable way of worshiping the true god is worship has given his church a large measure of liberty, within the rules of his word, so that all things are done decently and in order. the proper elements of a worship service are the reading of holy scripture, the singing of psalms and hymns, the offering of prayer, the preaching of the word, the presentation of offerings, confessing the faith, and observing the sacraments, with oaths on special occasions. god commanded his old testament people to keep the last day of the week holy, and sanctified the first day as the sabbath by the resurrection of christ, so that the church of the new dispensation has kept the first day holy since the time of the apostles. the whole day is to be kept holy and employed in the public and private exercises of religion, with a holy resting from unnecessary labours and from recreations lawful on other days. households are to order the day so that no one is improperly detained from public worship, and the time not spent in public worship is given to prayer, devotional reading and the study of scripture, meditation, catechizing, religious conversation, singing, visiting the sick, relieving the poor, teaching the ignorant and holy resting. title: Marriage, the Sick, Burial and the Home
blurb: The remaining chapters of the Directory, and the one section among them that is law.
text: marriage, the sick, burial and the home the remaining chapters of the directory, and the one section among them that is law. marriage is a divine institution, though not a sacrament and not peculiar to the church of christ. it is proper that every commonwealth should make laws to regulate marriage, which citizens are bound to obey so far as those laws do not transgress the laws of god. christians should marry in the lord, and it is fit that their marriage be solemnized by a lawful minister, with special instruction and suitable prayers. marriage is only to be between one man and one woman, in accordance with the word of god, and ministers in this church who solemnize marriages shall only solemnize marriages between one man and one woman. this section carries full constitutional authority. the parties should be of years of discretion, able to make their own choice, and where they are under age or live with parents the consent of those under whose care they are should be obtained and certified to the minister. parents should neither compel their children to marry against their inclinations nor withhold consent without just and important reasons. because marriage is of a public nature, its purpose should be sufficiently published beforehand, and ministers are to obey the laws of the community so far as those laws do not transgress the laws of god as the constitution of this church interprets them. the minister keeps a proper register of the marriages he performs. the power of the prayer of faith is great, and christians should make entreaty for the sick and seek god’s blessing on the means employed for recovery. when a person is sick, the minister or an officer of the church should be told, so that minister, officers and members may unite in prayer. it is the privilege and duty of the pastor to visit the sick and to minister to their physical, mental and spiritual welfare, using discretion in varying circumstances. the services proper at a burial are the singing of appropriate psalms or hymns, the reading of suitable portions of scripture with such remarks as seem proper to the minister, and prayer in which the bereaved are especially remembered. the service is left largely to the minister’s discretion, but its proper object is the worship of god and the consolation of the living. observing days of fasting and thanksgiving as providence directs is both scriptural and rational. they may be observed by individuals, families, particular congregations, groups of congregations, the congregations of a presbytery, or all the congregations of the church. individuals and families judge for themselves, sessions judge for congregations, presbyteries for larger districts, and where a fast or thanksgiving should be general the call is issued by the general assembly. besides public worship, it is the duty of each person in secret and of every family in private to worship god. secret worship is plainly enjoined by our lord, and includes prayer, form of outspoken recognition of god. parents instruct their children in the word and in the principles of religion, set an example of piety and consistent living, and cooperate with the church in the title: How the Constitution Changes
blurb: Three steps for the book, three-fourths at every step for the Standards, and where an idea starts.
text: how the constitution changes three steps for the book, three-fourths at every step for the standards, and where an idea starts. approval of the proposed amendment by a majority of those present and voting in the general assembly, and its recommendation to the presbyteries. the advice and consent of two-thirds of the presbyteries. approval and enactment by a subsequent general assembly, by a majority of those present and voting. in voting on an amendment, presbyteries may not divide its parts except as the assembly that recommended it directs. where enough presbyteries fail to act or to report that the response is unsatisfactory, the next assembly may defer action for a year and urge the delinquent presbyteries to report. the doctrinal standards are harder to move. amendment requires three-fourths of those present and voting in the assembly, then the advice and consent of three-fourths of the presbyteries, then approval and enactment by a subsequent assembly by three-fourths of those present and voting. the paragraph setting that rule can itself be amended only by the same method. full organic union with another ecclesiastical body follows the same three-fourths pattern at each of three steps, and that paragraph is likewise protected. receiving another body under the assembly’s jurisdiction, short of organic union, requires the consent of three-fourths of the presbyteries. an overture is ordinarily the request of a presbytery for action by the general assembly on a specific matter, and presbytery has power to propose to the assembly such measures as may be of common advantage to the church at large. all overtures are published in the commissioner handbook. overtures requesting amendment of the book of church order or the assembly’s rules go to the committee on constitutional business for its advice, and overtures proposing amendment of the constitution go to the overtures committee. the stated clerk’s referral is final unless the assembly redirects it by vote. so the practical path of a change runs: an idea, a presbytery that adopts it as an overture, a committee that studies it, an assembly that sends it down, the presbyteries that vote, and a second assembly that enacts it. a single assembly cannot alter the constitution by itself.

title: Beside Other Presbyterian Churches
blurb: Three points of comparison that were checked in each body’s own documents.
text: beside other presbyterian churches three points of comparison that were checked in each body’s own documents. this church has three courts: session, presbytery and general assembly. there are no synods. the presbyterian church (u.s.a.) has four councils: the session for the congregation, the presbytery for a district, the synod as an intermediate council for a region, and the general assembly for the whole church. in this church the assembly consists of all teaching elders in good standing, together with ruling elders elected by their sessions on a fixed formula. it is not a delegated body as to teaching elders. the orthodox presbyterian church has a delegated assembly of about 150 voting commissioners, ministers and ruling elders commissioned by their presbyteries, with the total fixed by standing rule and the ministerial share capped. in the presbyterian church (u.s.a.) the general assembly likewise consists of commissioners elected by presbyteries, half ruling elders and half teaching elders. in this church a congregation owns its property outright, with no right of reversion to any court, and may withdraw at any time for reasons sufficient to it, after at least thirty days notice of the meeting. in the presbyterian church (u.s.a.) all property held by or for a congregation is held in trust for the denomination, and the relationship of a congregation to the denomination may be severed only by constitutional action of the presbytery. this is the difference that most often reaches civil courts, and it is the one to state carefully, because it turns on the text of each body’s constitution rather than on temperament. rules on who may hold office in other denominations were not checked against their own constitutions for this course, so no comparison of that kind is offered here. the same caution applies to any claim about another body’s worship, discipline or doctrine: check that body’s own book before repeating it.

text: filing a complaint the route for a member who believes a court acted wrongly. check that complaint is the right remedy any communing member in good standing subject to the court may complain against any action of it. no complaint is allowable in a judicial case after process has commenced, though one filed then is held until the case ends. file with the court complained against written notice with supporting reasons, filed with that court’s clerk within sixty days following the meeting. the court considers it at its next stated meeting, or a called meeting before then, provided the complaint was filed at least ten days in advance. if denied, carry it up written notice filed with the clerks of both courts within thirty days of notification of the decision. the same route is open if the lower court fails to consider it. effect and hearing notice does not suspend the action unless a third of those present when it was taken so vote. the court complained against appoints representatives; the parties are complainant and respondent; the complainant opens and closes the argument. disposition the higher court may annul the whole or part of the action, or send the matter back with instructions for a new hearing.

title: Taking an appeal
blurb: The route for a party against whom judgment was rendered.
text: taking an appeal the route for a party against whom judgment was rendered. confirm standing appeal is open to those who submitted to a regular trial, those censured in a case without process, those whose censure was raised under 36-8, and those divested without censure under 34-10. notice notice may be given before the court adjourns. written notice with supporting reasons is filed with the clerks of both courts within thirty days of notification. the record goes up the clerk of the lower court files the record of the case within thirty days of receiving notice. nothing outside the record is considered without the consent of the parties. effect pending appeal the judgment is suspended, though the court of original jurisdiction may, for recorded reasons and by a two-thirds vote, keep the appellant from the table or from official functions, never as censure. hearing after the record is read, each side has not over thirty minutes, the appellant opening and closing. the court votes on each specification of error in turn. decision affirm in whole or part, reverse in whole or part, render the decision that should have been rendered, or remand for a new trial, always with a written opinion.

title: Organizing a mission church
blurb: From a gathering under supervision to a constituted church.
text: organizing a mission church from a gathering under supervision to a constituted church. presbytery establishes the work on its own initiative, at a session’s initiative, or on the written petition of an independent gathering. outside presbytery bounds, an assembly committee may exercise these powers. temporary government an evangelist, or a mother church session, or a commission serving as a temporary session, with records submitted to presbytery for annual review. members received under chapter 57 so far as it applies. those received are communing or non-communing members of this church, and rolls are kept separately. officers elected when qualified men appear, nomination and election follow chapter 24 so far as it applies, normally at least two weeks before the organization service, with the new officers taking office at its completion. petition and commission the members sign a petition to presbytery. on approval, presbytery appoints an organizing commission and sets the date and time of the service. the organization service officers are ordained and installed, a pastor may be ordained or installed, the members enter into covenant with uplifted hand, and the commission declares them constituted a church. first acts of the new session elect a stated clerk, form a budget, and where there is no pastor elect a moderator and act to secure the regular administration of word and sacraments.
